> 
> Iris (IR) is a chain of opticians in country K. Two years ago IR merged with a smaller rival that owned 25 shops, creating a business with 65 shops in total.
> 
> IR's directors expected the merger to achieve two objectives: to cut costs by buying frames and lenses in much larger quantities, and to raise market share to 30%.
> 
> The two businesses had worked in very different ways. IR had always allowed each shop manager to choose which frames to stock, while the smaller chain ordered everything centrally. Two years on, the two groups of shops still use separate ordering systems, and IR has not yet been able to place combined orders with its suppliers.
> 
> Nineteen optometrists have left IR since the merger. Several said they disliked the new working practices introduced afterwards.
>

>

> |---|---|

> | Market share now (%) | 24 |
> | Target market share (%) | 30 |
> | Cost of merging the two businesses so far (\$m) | 6.2 |

> 
> Rye (RY) owns 28 bakery shops in country L and also supplies bread to two supermarket chains. It employs 400 people and bakes everything at one central bakery.

> Flour is RY's largest single cost. RY buys all of its flour from three independent mills.

>

> 
> RY's directors are considering buying one of the three mills. Its owner is willing to sell for \$4.5m. The mill currently supplies RY and eleven other bakeries in country L.

> **[case-study]**
> **Harbour (HB)**
> 
> Harbour (HB) is a supermarket chain with 34 stores along the coast of country Q. It employs 1,400 people and is known for stocking fish and fresh produce from suppliers in the towns where its stores are located.
> 
> HB buys from around 200 small local suppliers. Many of these suppliers sell most of what they produce to HB.
> 
> A national supermarket group has offered to buy HB. The national group operates 600 stores across country Q, buys centrally from a small number of large suppliers, and sells at lower prices than HB.
> 
> HB's directors have recommended that shareholders accept the offer. Local newspapers have reported concern among shoppers and suppliers about what the sale would mean.

Explain **one** way the proposed takeover could affect HB's suppliers.
parts.solution_md:
One way the takeover could affect HB's suppliers is that many of them could lose their main customer **[1]**. The national group buys centrally from a small number of large suppliers, so it is unlikely to keep contracts with around 200 small local producers **[1]**. Because many of these suppliers sell most of what they produce to HB, losing that contract would threaten their survival rather than simply reduce their sales, and some may have to cut output or close altogether **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A takeover can affect suppliers through cancelled contracts, changed payment terms, pressure to reduce prices, larger order volumes, or greater certainty of payment from a bigger buyer
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The national group buys centrally from a small number of large suppliers, so most of HB's 200 local producers are unlikely to be retained
> - Many of these suppliers sell most of their output to HB, so losing the contract puts their survival at risk rather than simply reducing their revenue
> - Suppliers who are kept on may have to accept lower prices or longer payment periods, as a group with 600 stores has far greater bargaining power than HB
> - A small number of suppliers could gain if the national group offers access to all 600 of its stores, producing far larger orders than HB could ever place
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read carefully which group the question names. This one asks about suppliers, so points about shoppers or staff earn nothing however well argued. Underlining the stakeholder named in the question before you begin is a quick way to avoid throwing marks away.

> **Orbit (OB)**
> 
> Orbit (OB) manufactures cases, chargers and headphones for mobile phones in country R. It was set up eight years ago and employs 45 people at a single factory.
> 
> OB sells mainly to independent phone shops across country R. Demand for its products has grown steadily, and OB's factory now runs at 96% of its capacity. In the past year OB has turned down two large orders because it could not produce enough units in time.

> |---|---|

> | Capacity utilisation (%) | 96 |
> | Average cost per unit (\$) | 4.20 |
> | Orders refused in 2025 (units) | 60,000 |

> OB's owner is considering renting a second factory unit nearby.

Explain **one** reason why OB might want to grow.
parts.solution_md:
One reason OB might want to grow is to meet demand that it currently has to turn away **[1]**. OB's factory already runs at 96% of capacity, and in the past year it refused orders totalling 60,000 units **[1]**. By renting a second factory unit, OB could accept these orders rather than losing them, raising its revenue and reducing the risk that the independent phone shops it supplies find another manufacturer and stay with them permanently **[1]**

>

> **[case-study]**
> **Willow (WL)**
> 
> Willow (WL) owns six garden centres in country S. It sells plants, tools, compost and garden furniture, and each centre has a small cafe.
> 
> WL was started in 1971 by Grace Adeyemi, who opened a single plant nursery. It is now run by her daughter and two grandchildren, and the family still owns all of the shares. WL employs 210 people.
> 
> Several of WL's managers began as weekend staff and have worked for the business for more than twenty years. WL is well known in country S for the quality of its plants and for staff who can give expert gardening advice.
> 
> A national garden retailer has recently opened two large stores in the same region, selling similar products at lower prices.

Explain **one** strength of WL being a family business.
parts.solution_md:
One strength of WL being a family business is that decisions can be made quickly **[1]**. WL is owned entirely by Grace Adeyemi's daughter and two grandchildren, so they can agree a change between themselves without consulting outside shareholders **[1]**. This speed matters now that a national garden retailer has opened two large stores in the same region, because WL can adjust its prices or its range of plants far sooner than a competitor whose managers must wait for approval from head office **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Strengths include quick decision-making, a long-term outlook, shared values and commitment, strong staff loyalty, and a reputation built on the family name
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Ownership rests with three family members, so decisions can be agreed without consulting outside shareholders - valuable now that a national retailer has opened nearby and WL must respond
> - The family is not under pressure to deliver short-term profit to investors, so it can keep investing in plant quality and staff expertise that take years to repay
> - Managers who started as weekend staff and stayed over twenty years show the loyalty family firms often build, and their expert advice is one of the few things the cheaper national retailer cannot match
> - WL's reputation in country S is tied to the Adeyemi family name, giving the owners a personal reason to protect standards rather than cut costs to compete on price
>

> Meridian (MR) is a coach travel company in country T. It runs scheduled services between towns and cities, and hires out coaches for school trips and private tours.
> 
> MR owns a fleet of 48 coaches, kept at two depots. It employs 90 people, most of whom are drivers. Because modern coaches are expensive to buy, MR has a large amount of money tied up in its fleet compared with many businesses employing a similar number of people.

> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 14 |
> | Capital employed (\$m) | 22 |

> 
> MR's Managing Director has been asked to compare MR with a rival coach operator that employs 260 people but owns only 20 coaches, because it hires the rest.

Explain **one** method that could be used to measure the size of MR.
parts.solution_md:
One method of measuring the size of MR is capital employed **[1]**. MR has \$22m of capital employed, which is high compared with its revenue of \$14m because coaches are expensive to buy **[1]**. This measure suits MR better than counting employees, because the rival operator employs 260 people but hires most of its coaches, so it would appear larger by headcount even though MR owns far more of the assets it uses **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
>

> 
> AO1
> 
> - Methods include number of employees, revenue, capital employed, market share, and the number of units of equipment or outlets owned
>

>

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** reason why a business might choose to remain small.
parts.solution_md:
One reason a business might choose to remain small is to keep close personal contact with its customers **[1]**. In a small business the owner usually serves customers directly and can remember their individual preferences **[1]**. This kind of personal service becomes much harder to maintain as a business grows and employs more staff, so staying small allows the owner to keep the loyal customers who value being known and dealt with personally **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Reasons include keeping close contact with customers, retaining full control, avoiding diseconomies of scale, limited finance for expansion, serving a niche market, and the owner preferring a manageable workload
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Personal service is easier to provide when the owner deals with customers directly, and customers who value this are more likely to stay loyal and recommend the business
> - Remaining small allows the owner to keep full control of decisions rather than sharing it with investors or delegating to managers who may not share their priorities
> - Larger businesses can suffer diseconomies of scale such as poor communication and weaker motivation, which raise average costs - staying small avoids these
> - A business serving a niche market may find there are too few customers to justify growth, so expanding would raise costs without a proportionate rise in revenue
>

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'strategic alliance'.
parts.solution_md:
A strategic alliance is an agreement between two or more businesses to work together on a particular project **[1]**, while each remains a separate and independent business **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
>

> 
> - An arrangement in which businesses co-operate to achieve a shared objective while remaining independent of one another
> - A partnership in which firms pool resources or expertise for a specific purpose without forming a new company
> - An agreement to work together, for example on research or distribution, which does not involve either business buying a share of the other

> **[exam-tip]**
> With two marks available, give two distinct pieces of information rather than one idea expressed twice. Here that means saying what the businesses do together and saying that they stay independent. Writing your definition as two clear clauses makes both marks easy to award.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'hostile takeover'.
parts.solution_md:
A hostile takeover is when one business buys another **[1]** against the wishes of the directors of the business being bought **[1]**

>

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'horizontal integration'.
parts.solution_md:
Horizontal integration is when a business merges with or takes over another business **[1]** that operates at the same stage of the same industry **[1]**

parts.problem_md:
‘Marketing is the most important factor for the success of small businesses.’

Discuss the extent to which you agree with this view.
parts.solution_md:
Marketing involves identifying and satisfying customer needs profitably **[K]**. For a small business, it is undeniably important - without customers, there is no revenue. A new small business is largely unknown **[Ap]**, so marketing creates awareness and communicates its value proposition **[An]**. In a competitive market, effective marketing helps attract customers away from larger competitors, and digital and social media marketing makes this relatively affordable for businesses with limited budgets **[An]**

However, many small businesses fail not because of poor marketing but because of inadequate cash flow management **[K]**. A business can attract customers through effective marketing but still fail if it cannot pay suppliers, employees or rent on time. Sound financial management - monitoring cash flow and controlling costs **[K] **- is arguably more fundamental to short-term survival, particularly in the early stages when cash is scarce and margins are tight  **[Ap]** **[An]**

Product quality **[K] **is also critical. If a small business cannot consistently deliver what it promises, marketing can accelerate its failure by raising customer expectations it cannot meet **[Ap]**. Negative online reviews damage reputation quickly and are difficult to recover from. A business with a genuinely distinctive product may need very little formal marketing - satisfied customers generate recommendations that drive growth organically at no cost **[An]**

Overall, marketing is important but is unlikely to be the single most important factor for the success of small businesses **[E]**. Its significance depends on the stage of the business: in the short term, financial management and operational quality are more critical - a business must first stay solvent and deliver reliably before marketing can have any meaningful impact **[An]**. Marketing becomes the most important factor once these foundations are in place and the business needs to grow and compete in the market. For most small businesses, survival must come before growth **[Ap]** **[E]**

> | **4** | 15-16 | - Limited evaluation of the extent to which you agree with the view that marketing is the most important factor for the success of small businesses |
> | **3** | 11-14 | - Good analysis of the extent to which you agree with the view that marketing is the most important factor for the success of small businesses |
> | **2** | 5-10 | - Limited analysis, with application, of the view that marketing is important to the success of small businesses |
> | **1** | 1-4 | - Knowledge and understanding of marketing/small businesses |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> Arguments for marketing being the most important factor
> 
> - Marketing creates awareness of a small business and communicates its value proposition to potential customers. Without customers there is no revenue, so attracting and retaining them is fundamental to success. A new small business is largely unknown, making marketing essential for establishing itself in the market
> - Effective marketing helps a small business differentiate itself from larger, better-resourced competitors. If a small business cannot compete on price, it must compete on perceived value - communicating quality, uniqueness or personal service through targeted promotion
> - Digital and social media marketing is relatively low-cost and accessible, meaning small businesses can reach large audiences without the significant budgets required for traditional advertising. This partially levels the playing field with larger competitors
> - Marketing sustains customer relationships and encourages repeat business, which is often the primary revenue source for small businesses. Loyal customers also generate word-of-mouth referrals, which costs nothing but can be highly effective
> 
> Arguments against marketing being the most important factor
> 
> - Many small businesses fail due to poor cash flow management rather than poor marketing. A business can attract customers through effective marketing but still collapse if it cannot pay suppliers, employees or rent on time. Financial management is arguably more fundamental to survival, particularly in the early stages
> - The quality of the product or service is critical. If a business cannot consistently deliver what it promises, marketing raises customer expectations it cannot meet - accelerating its failure through negative reviews and damaged reputation. A distinctive, high-quality product may generate sufficient word-of-mouth with very little formal marketing
> - Skilled management and operational efficiency are also essential. Poor decision-making, weak record-keeping, or inability to scale operations will undermine any marketing success
> - The economic environment can outweigh the impact of marketing entirely. In a recession, reduced consumer spending may mean that even highly effective marketing cannot generate sufficient demand to keep a small business viable
> 
> Evaluation
> 
> - The relative importance of marketing depends on the stage of the business. In the short term, financial management and product quality are more critical to survival. Marketing becomes the most important factor once the business is financially stable and needs to grow its customer base
> - The degree of competition matters. In a crowded market, marketing may be the key differentiator; in a niche market with little competition, operational quality and financial management may matter more.
> - A balanced conclusion might argue that marketing is a necessary but not sufficient condition for success - it amplifies a well-run business but cannot compensate for poor financial management, weak products or operational failure.
> - The time horizon of "success" is also relevant: short-term survival depends most on cash flow; long-term growth depends more on marketing and brand building
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

The cost of developing the VR ride would be \$2m. The Iron Blaster ride would be closed for a three-month period during the off-peak season for the development to be carried out.
